catalog_quote: §. 2. Spostamenti di accento. 1. In generale l'accento in bolognese si mantiene sulla sillaba che lo ha in latino o in italiano. Tuttavia vi sono importanti eccezioni a questa regola. 2. Nella coniugazione dei verbi, l'analogia delle altre persone dello stesso tempo fa sì, che la prima e seconda persona plurale ritraggano l'accento dalla desinenza sul tema nell'imperfetto dell'indicativo: êren, êri (erámus erátis), cantæven cantævi ..., e nell'imperfetto del congiuntivo, ciò che è però comune anche all'italiano: fossen, fossi (fuissémus, fuissétis). ... Nel perfetto forte dell'indicativo invece, la prima persona in bolognese ha l'accento sulla vocale del tema come in latino: dessen dicemmo, da diximus, vesten vedemmo, da vidimus. 3. Tuttavia vi sono importanti eccezioni a questa regola. 2. Nella coniugazione dei verbi, l'analogia delle altre persone dello stesso tempo fa sì, che la prima e seconda persona plurale ritraggano l'accento dalla desinenza sul tema nell'imperfetto dell'indicativo: éren, èri (eràmus eràtis) [...] 4. new_statements.translation: §2. Shifts of accent. 1. In general the accent in Bolognese is kept on the syllable that bears it in Latin or in Italian. There are however important exceptions to this rule. 2. In verb conjugation, analogy with the other persons of the same tense causes the first and second person plural to retract the accent from the ending onto the stem in the imperfect indicative: éren, èri (eràmus eràtis) [...] 4. When an etymological i or u is retained in the penultimate syllable of an originally paroxytone word, the accent moves onto it: pzìg 'pizzico' [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is inherited: it stays on the syllable stressed in Latin/Italian, so it is lexically fixed and not predictable from the surface word (after apocope and syncope the same lexical stress yields many oxytones and paroxytones); this is a fixed-stress Romance system like Italian, with listed lexical/morphological exceptions (analogical retraction in 1/2pl imperfects, shift onto a retained penultimate i/u, Latin -íolus > stress on the following vowel).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Gaudenzi. Cavirani 2015 (p. 33 area) discusses etymological secondary stress only in the proto-Romance background.
new_statements.exceptions: Gaudenzi §2 nn. 2-5: analogical stress retraction in 1st/2nd plural imperfect indicative and subjunctive (éren, èri; fossen, fossi), stress kept on the stem in strong perfects (dessen, vesten), Latin proparoxytones in -i(V) shifting stress to the following vowel (filiolus > fiôl), stress moved onto a retained penultimate etymological i/u (pzìg, biasùff), and apparent exceptions from popular reformations (arpatg, insìda, cariga, intîr).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of Bolognese city dialect (Glottolog bolo1260); stressed vowels are long or short by quantity rules (§1 pp. 60-61). Ferretti 2007 (Reggiano) adds that clitic monosyllables are unstressed within the phrase (per mé pronounced as one word). Cavirani 2015 (Lunigiano) states only that Romance stress position is lexically determined.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the city dialect of Bologna (Glottolog dialect bolo1260 'Bologna Emiliano' under emil1241), as spoken in the 1880s. The other opened descriptions cover Reggiano (Ferretti 2007, cent1959 area), Novellara (Malagoli 1913), Modena (Bertoni 1905/1925), the Bolognese Apennine (Vitali), and Lunigiano/Carrarese-Pontremolese (Cavirani 2015, luni1238); none contradicts the etymological-stress statement.

V 'Quantità e accento', §2 'Spostamenti di accento', p. 62 (PDF p. 120): in general Bolognese keeps the accent on the syllable that bears it in Latin or Italian; lists exceptions (analogical retraction in 1/2pl imperfect, shift onto a retained i/u in the penult, etc.). §1 pp. 60-61: stressed-vowel length rules.

sources.citation: Cavirani, Edoardo. 2015. Modeling phonologization: Vowel reduction and epenthesis in Lunigiana dialects (LOT 384). Utrecht: LOT. [Carrarese and Pontremolese = Lunigiano luni1238]

sources.note: Ch. 2 gives stressed vs unstressed vowel inventories of Pontremolese (2.2.2) and Carrarese (2.3.2, p. 25) and says post-tonic unstressed vowels are generally deleted, pretonic ones partly retained; the only placement statement is diachronic background, p. 33: 'By the beginning of 5th century, then, the stress position is lexically determined' (proto-Romance, citing Loporcaro 2011a). No dialect-specific placement rule.

sources.citation: Ferretti, Denis. 2007. Grammatica reggiana (prefazione di Daniele Vitali), online, 120 pp. bulgnais.com.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 2-3: stressed vowels of Reggiano are long or short, open or closed, every tonic vowel written with an accent; unstressed vowels bear no accent; clitic monosyllables behave as unstressed within the phrase. p. 12 'L'accento' is orthographic (monosyllabic verbs in -a written with accent). pp. 15ff: verb-root vowel alternation depends on whether stress falls on root or ending. No general placement rule.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Historical phonology organised by Latin tonic/atonic vowels; §62 (p. 31): Modenese shares with Emilian dialects the loss of every final unstressed vowel except -a; §70-71: syncope of post-tonic medial vowels reduces dactyls to trochaic accentuation. No synchronic placement rule (confirms earlier scan).
